channel_name: Invest Like the Best · Patrick O'Shaughnessy
video_title: Why the World Order Is Collapsing and American Power Is Rising
gist: Historian Walter Russell Mead (author of 'Special Providence' and 'God and Gold', WSJ Global View columnist) argues to Patrick O'Shaughnessy that the post-1945 rules-based order is collapsing under Trump even as underlying American tech-driven power strengthens, and walks through concrete near-term risk markers: Taiwan gray-zone/soft-blockade tactics, Japan's remilitarization, Iran's shift toward threatening Gulf desalination plants, China's energy stockpiling as war-hedge, and the unverifiable danger of bio/cyber WMDs.

themes.theme: Fraying Order and Trump's Power Method

insights.claim: The post-1945 'Pax Americana' institutional order (WTO rules-based trade, NATO, the UN) is in acute crisis and actively crumbling, even as underlying American power -- driven by the information revolution and rising productivity -- continues to strengthen, producing a split picture of a dynamic country inside a collapsing world system.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Investors should not conflate the erosion of multilateral institutions with US decline -- American economic/tech strength may be a better forward indicator than institutional stability.
insights.quote: it's this odd picture of a dynamic country and a collapsing world system.

insights.claim: Trump has abandoned the traditional US posture of being 'steady and predictable' in foreign policy (honoring commitments made decades earlier without fanfare) in favor of deliberate unpredictability and explicit threats, such as threatening to double tariffs on allies who don't raise defense spending -- a shift Mead says will be very difficult for successors to reverse because it is dismantling the institutional channels that carried American power for 80 years.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Tariff/policy unpredictability under Trump is a structural regime change in how the US exercises power, not a temporary tactic -- raises the baseline geopolitical/tariff risk premium for multinationals even after Trump leaves office.
insights.quote: he's now he's he's completely trashing the institutional networks that for a very long time were the vessels of American power.

insights.claim: Trump's core political innovation, per Mead, is converting fame and spectacle directly into political power that is immune to normal reputational constraints -- because the marginal cost of repeated lies falls toward zero, and because Bill Clinton first proved that political shame only has power if the leader lets it. Trump has deployed this insight 'on an industrial scale.'
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Investors modeling political/headline risk from Trump should expect conventional scandal-based mean-reversion signals (approval collapse, resignation pressure) to be far weaker predictors than in past administrations.
insights.quote: if you lie enough the marginal cost of your 10,000th lie is nothing while the marginal law of your first second or third the marginal cost is very high.

insights.claim: Mead sees a broader global realignment toward personalized, non-bureaucratic 'strongman' politics -- citing Modi (India), Abe (Japan), Netanyahu (Israel), Erdogan (Turkey), Putin (Russia), Xi Jinping (China), and Trump (US) as the same phenomenon, which he attributes partly to an internet-era public wanting to be 'ruled by people again' rather than by institutions and committees.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Political-risk models across India, Japan, Israel, Turkey, Russia, China and the US should weight single-leader idiosyncratic risk and policy volatility more heavily than institutional-continuity assumptions.
insights.quote: I think one of the impacts of the internet is that people want to be ruled by people again.

themes.theme: Maritime Commercial Playbook vs. Continental Powers

insights.claim: Mead's 300-year historical pattern (summarized in his book 'God and Gold' as 'UP to UK to US' -- United Provinces, United Kingdom, United States) holds that open, commercial, maritime powers have repeatedly defeated larger, more centralized continental land powers (Louis XIV's France, Napoleonic France, Wilhelmine/Nazi Germany, the Soviet Union), and he frames today's US-China rivalry as the latest iteration, with China cast as the technocratic continental challenger.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Provides a long-duration historical base rate favoring the US/allied maritime-commercial bloc over China in a protracted strategic competition -- a useful prior for long-horizon geopolitical risk allocation.
insights.quote: you could sum up the last 300 years of modern history in 10 letters, UP, United Provinces to UK to US.

insights.claim: The historical winning playbook Mead describes has three steps: (1) maintain an open, tolerant domestic society that attracts talent and permits entrepreneurial risk-taking; (2) use resulting innovation to trade globally and accumulate wealth; and (3) -- unlike closed extractive empires such as Spain in colonial Latin America -- invite rivals and partners into your trading system, which grows everyone richer but also makes them structurally dependent on you.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Explains why US-led globalization deliberately included rivals (post-Cold War Russia and China) as a strategic policy choice, not naivety -- relevant to assessing whether re-decoupling from China forfeits a proven strategic advantage.

insights.claim: The dependence created by inclusion in an open trading system becomes a wartime weapon: Germany's growing reliance on imported Argentine/American grain and Malayan rubber before WWI let Britain cripple it via blockade once war began -- a precedent Mead implies is directly analogous to how a US-led counter-blockade could cripple China's economy, which depends on imported oil, soybeans, and export markets, in a Taiwan conflict scenario.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: In a Taiwan crisis, expect the primary US leverage to be economic/trade blockade rather than direct military confrontation -- implications for shipping, commodities (oil, soybeans), and Chinese-import-dependent supply chains.

insights.claim: Mead states directly that a top fear keeping Xi Jinping 'awake at night' is that in any US-China conflict, China would be cut off from the raw materials and export markets its economy depends on -- illustrated by a hypothetical where China blockades Taiwan and the US imposes a wider counter-blockade halting Chinese oil imports, manufactured exports, and Brazilian/Argentine soybean deliveries.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: China's Taiwan calculus is constrained more by economic-blockade vulnerability than by direct military risk -- a key variable for handicapping Taiwan-conflict probability and China trade/commodity exposure.
insights.quote: If there are things that keep Xi Jinping awake at night, I think one of them is his awareness that in any kind of conflict with the United States, China would face being cut off from so many of the raw materials.

insights.claim: Mead expresses high personal conviction that China cannot ultimately overtake the US in the great-power contest.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: A high-profile foreign-policy historian's base case is US-favorable over the long run, running counter to the more common 'China inevitability' narrative -- worth weighing against China-bear vs. China-bull portfolio tilts.
insights.quote: I don't think China has it in in it to beat us.

insights.claim: China's aggressive build-out of solar, hydro, and coal capacity, plus unusually large oil stockpiles only recently made visible by the Iran war, should be read primarily as a strategic hedge to reduce dependence on global energy/commodity markets in case of a US conflict -- not, as much Western environmental commentary assumes, primarily a green-energy/decarbonization choice.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: China's renewable/energy buildout should be modeled as strategic-autarky capex rather than purely climate-driven demand -- affects how investors interpret Chinese commodity and clean-energy equipment demand signals.
insights.quote: what they're trying to do is make themselves less dependent on the outside world so that in a worst case scenario with the US, they can actually fight for the long term.

insights.claim: On Taiwan, Mead argues Xi is not operating on a fixed deadline and that China needs very high confidence of success before committing to invasion because failure would be catastrophic; the more likely near-term moves are gray-zone/soft-blockade tactics, such as requiring ships bound for Taiwan to first clear a Chinese port for customs, designed to assert sovereignty without triggering a direct US/allied military response.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Investors hedging Taiwan risk should price a higher probability of gradual gray-zone coercion (shipping/insurance/logistics disruption) over the next few years versus a discrete invasion event.
insights.quote: they're trying to get themselves into a position where they could have a soft blockade where like they could give the orders that any ship that wants to go to Taiwan first has to stop at a Chinese port.

insights.claim: Mead identifies Japan's strategic awakening -- increased defense spending, doctrinal rethinking, and viewing Chinese control of Taiwan as a direct existential threat to its own independence -- as the 'big new factor' investors should track, since how fast Japan builds credible deterrent capability will directly shape China's Taiwan risk calculus.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Japanese defense-budget trajectory and doctrine changes are a leading indicator for Taiwan-conflict probability -- worth monitoring alongside direct China/Taiwan signals.
insights.quote: The big new factor is that the Japanese have woken up and the Japanese see would see Chinese control of Taiwan as a direct threat to Japanese independence.

insights.claim: Ukraine's success at keeping the much larger Russian Black Sea Navy out of the Black Sea using inexpensive drones, despite having no real navy of its own, is 'good news for Taiwan' -- suggesting an asymmetric, drone-heavy defense strategy could plausibly deny Chinese naval superiority around Taiwan without Taiwan needing a blue-water navy.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Supports an investment/policy thesis favoring cheap asymmetric drone/anti-ship capability procurement for Taiwan over expensive legacy naval platforms -- relevant to defense-sector positioning toward drone/loitering-munition makers over traditional shipbuilders.
insights.quote: They have kept the Russian Navy out of the Black Sea with drones. Good news for Taiwan actually.

insights.claim: Mead argues the US, as the power with the largest stock of legacy military platforms (tanks, large surface navy), is structurally the most exposed to rapid military-technology obsolescence from drone warfare -- more so than adversaries who never built up those legacy systems in the first place.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Counterintuitive risk framing for defense investors: incumbency in legacy platforms (tanks, carriers) is now a liability, not a moat -- favors reallocation toward drone/autonomous-systems defense suppliers over traditional heavy-platform primes.
insights.quote: we've got more we got so many tanks that the tank becomes useless. That's more of a problem for us than it is for somebody who's figured out the tank killer.

insights.claim: Mead frames the imbalance of power in Asia as driven less by China's absolute size than by the growth gap between China and its neighbors -- India's GDP was roughly 60-65% of China's in 1980 versus roughly 17% today -- and argues the US strategic goal should be helping India, Indonesia, and Vietnam grow enough that China cannot dominate all of Asia, rather than trying to contain China militarily alone.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Reframes the US-China strategic competition as partly an India/Indonesia/Vietnam growth-and-investment story -- a supportive thesis for continued foreign capital allocation to these three economies as a geopolitical hedge/complement to China exposure.
insights.quote: in 1980 India's GDP was something like 60% 65% of China's today it's about 17% of China's.

themes.theme: AI, Tech Power, and the New Competitive Moats

insights.claim: Mead observes that 20 years ago the world's top 10-20 market-cap companies were a diverse global mix across industries, whereas today that list is dominated almost entirely by American technology companies, with OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX now layering on top of already-dominant incumbents as a fresh wave of US tech leadership.
insights.speaker: Patrick O'Shaughnessy (host)
insights.so_what: Confirms and extends the 'US tech exceptionalism' thesis behind concentrated US equity index weightings -- worth watching whether new frontier AI labs eventually join public top-20 market-cap ranks.
insights.quote: Now that same list is literally just American technology companies, like basically one through 20.

insights.claim: Unlike physical infrastructure such as railroads and highways that rivals cannot simply copy, frontier AI capability can be 'distilled' by competitors like China without matching the original capital investment -- Mead flags this as a fundamentally weaker economies-of-scale dynamic than past infrastructure-based hegemonies, complicating traditional foreign-policy thinking about tech leadership.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Frontier AI labs' moats may be shorter-lived than historically assumed given distillation/replication risk -- relevant to how investors value AI-lab equity/IP durability and to the policy case for export controls on model weights/compute.
insights.quote: they're able to distil... have fairly comparable systems without the capital investment which is very different than like the highway system or the railroads.

insights.claim: Mead introduces 'infostructure' as the missing complement to physical infrastructure -- the institutional, legal, and regulatory framework needed for AI to actually deliver value in complex domains like hospital care or the legal system -- arguing this social/regulatory buildout, not the raw technology, is the current bottleneck to realizing AI's economic potential.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Investors should watch regulatory/legal-framework reform (healthcare AI approval pathways, legal-system AI adoption rules) as the binding constraint and catalyst for AI monetization in regulated verticals, not just model capability improvements.
insights.quote: Infosstructure is the institutional legal regulatory framework that can allow AI technology to to develop give better results to patients in a hospital.

insights.claim: Mead argues US tech/AI companies need scale beyond the domestic US market to generate enough revenue and growth to remain even technologically equal to China, let alone stay ahead and profitable -- an argument against protectionist policies that would restrict US AI firms' access to global markets.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Supports a bullish read on continued international expansion/market access for US AI leaders (compute, cloud, model licensing) as strategically necessary, not optional -- relevant to assessing risk of trade or export-control policies that cut off US AI firms' foreign revenue.
insights.quote: if our AI companies, if our tech companies can only benefit from the internal American market, that's actually not enough to generate the revenue and growth that they need even to stay technologically equal, say, to China.

insights.claim: Mead flags a live and unresolved policy debate over whether to automate national-security/nuclear decision-making with AI to strengthen deterrence credibility (an adversary knows retaliation is certain if triggers are automated), versus retaining human decision points that introduce hesitation but avoid a literal 'doomsday machine.'
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: An emerging AI-safety/defense-policy debate (automated retaliation vs. human-in-the-loop) that could shape defense-AI contracting and nuclear-command-and-control modernization spending.
insights.quote: are we will really willing to have the doomsday machine decide whether we're going to go to war or use nuclear weapons or something like that?

insights.claim: Tech firms in the 1990s explicitly self-identified as stateless global companies, but Mead says tech is now 'the locus of international great power competition,' driving an unexpected mutual realignment between Silicon Valley and Washington.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Explains the structural basis for continued/expanding US tech-sector alignment with national-security policy (export controls, CFIUS scrutiny, government AI partnerships) as a durable trend, not a temporary political phase.
insights.quote: Today, tech is actually the locus of international great power competition.

insights.claim: Mead argues tech companies' economic interests differ structurally from legacy multinationals: legacy manufacturers need open trade, labor, and financial markets everywhere, while tech firms care far more about intellectual-property security and supply-chain security than about cheap immigrant labor, and increasingly need employees who view selling IP to China as a serious wrong -- a shift he calls the rise of 'tech Hamiltonians.'
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Predicts continued tech-sector political support for IP-protection/export-control policy even where it conflicts with older Silicon Valley open-immigration/open-trade orthodoxy -- relevant to handicapping tech lobbying positions on China policy.
insights.quote: companies are starting to realize that they need their employees to be patriotic... your co-workers will rat you out in a heartbeat if they think you're doing something like that.

insights.claim: Mead argues the industrial revolution forced civilizational convergence toward Western institutional models because mass manufacturing required similar infrastructure everywhere, but the information/AI revolution is instead enabling civilizational divergence, letting countries use their own languages and cultures as platforms -- citing Turkey as 'more Turkish' and India and Japan as becoming more themselves than 25 years ago, using MTV Latin America's shift from American rock videos to local artists as the historical analogy.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Investors should expect AI-driven media/content and platform strategies to fragment along national/cultural lines rather than homogenize globally -- favors localized content, language-specific AI models, and national platforms over one-size-fits-all global products.
insights.quote: I think we're seeing a lot of that now where instead of having to be on the mainline programming of global programming, you're much freer to go off into your own civilization.

insights.claim: Mead sees India as an increasingly important, distinct third pole in global power, underpinned by the BJP/RSS Hindu-nationalist movement's roughly 86,000 grassroots cells meeting weekly across India, and notes India explicitly rejects both the status quo and the Chinese authoritarian model, per Foreign Minister Jaishankar's framing that China is a revisionist power while India is a reformist power, while resenting its structural under-representation at the UN despite having 1.4 billion people and nuclear weapons but the same one vote as Liechtenstein or Luxembourg.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: India's political durability is grounded in deep grassroots organizational infrastructure, not just Modi personally -- supports continued conviction in India as a structurally stable, distinct growth/investment pole separate from a China-alignment bet.
insights.quote: China is a revisionist power India is a reformist power.

insights.claim: Mead flags the Islamic world, spanning sophisticated Gulf and Turkish elites to more radical elements in North Africa, as a growing, heterogeneous force whose internal cultural evolution -- particularly in the Gulf states and Turkey -- deserves closer investor/analyst attention as a distinct axis of global change beyond the US-China binary.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: A reminder not to reduce global power analysis purely to a US-China bipolar frame; Gulf/Turkish cultural and political evolution is an underweighted variable worth independent tracking.

themes.theme: Modern Warfare, WMD Risk, and Deterrence Erosion

insights.claim: Based on repeated visits to Ukraine, Mead describes a battlefield transformed by drones into a 'gray kill zone' where combat is no longer battalion-versus-battalion but scattered pairs of soldiers, medics report they no longer treat bullet wounds because injuries are now almost all drone-caused, and casualty evacuation has become one of the hardest problems in the war, requiring dedicated armored ground-drone teams protected by escort drones, with one soldier reportedly taking 63 days to be evacuated after being wounded.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Concrete, current evidence that drone saturation has structurally changed frontline casualty/evacuation dynamics -- relevant to defense-tech investment theses around casualty-evacuation robotics and counter-drone systems, and to modeling attrition rates in future conflicts.
insights.quote: They told me they had one soldier that it took them 63 days to get them evacuated after a wound.

insights.claim: Mead argues that unlike the discrete 1990s-era 'revolution in military affairs,' the current environment is one of continuing revolutions in military affairs -- meaning battlefield advantage, such as Ukraine's current edge, can flip within months, requiring militaries to continuously re-adapt rather than modernize once.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Defense procurement and force-structure planning should assume a continuously shifting technology frontier rather than a stable post-modernization equilibrium -- favors software-defined/iterable defense platforms over long-cycle hardware programs.
insights.quote: we've shifted now to... continuing revolutions in military affairs.

insights.claim: Mead argues nuclear proliferation, while still unsolved, is at least generally detectable with enough lead time to respond, whereas bioweapons and cyberweapons can be developed covertly in a basement lab with no reliable way to verify compliance with any arms-control agreement -- making the coming era of accelerating multi-domain arms races unusually dangerous given the near-total lack of strategic verifiability.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Reframes catastrophic tail risk away from nuclear proliferation, which is well-monitored, toward bio/cyber weapons, which are unverifiable -- relevant to biosecurity policy, dual-use biotech regulation, and long-tail insurance/catastrophe-risk modeling.
insights.quote: How could you verify whether somebody was abiding by some sort of cyber arms control agreement or boweapons arms control when basically in a basement lab somewhere you can cook up a pathogen that could destroy half the planet?

themes.theme: Middle East: Iran, the Gulf, and the Strait of Hormuz

insights.claim: Mead traces the collapse of pan-Arab nationalism, from Nasser's Egypt in the 1950s through the post-1967 decline and the more recent collapse of the Iraqi and Syrian states, as having left a power vacuum in the Middle East that Iran filled by building a 'Shia crescent' from Lebanon through Syria and Iraq into Iran -- a network that has since fractured following Israel's actions since October 7, though the underlying military weakness of the Gulf Arab states relative to Iran has not gone away.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Frames the current Gulf security order as structurally fragile even post-October 7 -- the Gulf states' wealth and oil leverage does not translate into independent military deterrence against Iran, keeping outside-power backing (the US) a load-bearing assumption in any Gulf investment thesis.

insights.claim: Mead argues the real emerging Iranian threat to the Gulf is no longer just drone strikes on individual oil tankers but the capability to target desalination plants, which could render Gulf cities essentially uninhabitable -- a threat that, left unresolved, chills the foreign investment underpinning Gulf states' economic-diversification megaprojects.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: A specific, underappreciated tail risk (desalination-infrastructure attack) that investors in Gulf diversification megaprojects and regional real estate/infrastructure should price into risk premiums.
insights.quote: it's it's not even as important that Iran can hit a tanker with a drone as it is that Iran could could put some drones on some uh desolinization plants and make the cities of the Gulf essentially uninhabitable.

insights.claim: Mead argues the US has been fundamentally unwilling, since the Obama administration, to draw and enforce a real red line against Iran in the Gulf/Strait of Hormuz, preferring to kick the can down the road, and that this erosion of credible deterrence -- mirrored in the Russia-Ukraine context -- reflects an absence of Truman/FDR-style political leadership capable of building durable public support for enforced commitments.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: Persistent US deterrence-credibility erosion toward Iran raises the structural risk premium on Strait of Hormuz oil-flow disruption over the medium term, independent of any single incident.
insights.quote: the United States has been fundamentally unwilling to do that itself and is looking, we want to kick the can down the road.

themes.theme: Domestic Political Economy and the AI Health Dividend

insights.claim: Mead proposes that remote/hybrid work and eventual self-driving cars could unlock a new multi-decade wave of housing supply by expanding the practical commuting radius, since developable land area scales with the square of the radius -- expanding a commute range from 40 to 75 miles dramatically increases buildable land -- framing this as the next iteration of the Homestead Act/highway-subsidy playbook that historically solved American housing-affordability crises.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: A structural, policy-actionable thesis for solving housing affordability via remote-work-enabled exurban expansion -- supportive of long-horizon investment in secondary/tertiary metro housing markets and remote-work-enabling infrastructure/technology.
insights.quote: If you expand the commuting radius, say from 40 miles to 75 miles, right? The amount of land that is developable for housing goes up with the square of the radius.

insights.claim: Mead suggests tax incentives for companies that adopt greater hybrid/remote work could be fiscally net-neutral or positive for government, since reduced office/commuting infrastructure wear-and-tear offsets the tax-revenue cost, using the example of a company allowing 60% remote work reducing associated infrastructure spending needs.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: A specific, testable fiscal-policy mechanism (hybrid-work tax credits funded by infrastructure savings) that could be a low-cost lever for housing/affordability policy -- worth watching for legislative uptake.
insights.quote: A tax benefit for companies that move toward greater hybrid and remote work actually is is not a net cost for government because in fact you're you're saving on another another part of the budget.

insights.claim: Mead argues the mid-20th-century American social structure rested on three now-collapsed stabilizing classes -- a unionized industrial working class, a professionally managed and heavily regulated oligopoly business class, and a technocratic expert/regulatory class -- and that this simultaneous breakdown, occurring exactly as AI-driven disruption accelerates, leaves the US without institutional shock absorbers just when it needs them most.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: A structural political-instability thesis: the US is entering the AI disruption era with unusually weak institutional buffers, raising the probability of disruptive domestic policy swings around AI, labor, and antitrust -- relevant to political-risk premia on US domestic policy exposure.
insights.quote: all three of those classes are in total disarray and yet we are facing a whole series of very serious changes perplexities... we're we're not organized to answer these in the old ways so we are really out at sea.

insights.claim: Mead argues AI-accelerated medical research is driving a 'cost revolution' in healthcare that could make US entitlement-program deficits, such as Medicare, substantially more solvable over the coming decades than currently assumed, since better and cheaper treatments would both extend healthy life and reduce per-capita care costs.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: A genuinely bullish, underweighted long-duration fiscal thesis: AI/biotech-driven healthcare cost deflation could materially ease the entitlement-driven federal deficit trajectory that dominates most long-term US fiscal bear cases.
insights.quote: I also believe that we're going to be seeing a cost revolution in health care... I think this means that things like the federal deficit due to entitlement programs are actually solvable.

insights.claim: As a concrete illustration of accelerating oncology drug development, Mead cites his friend Ben Sasse, diagnosed with terminal pancreatic cancer, being kept alive and functional by a drug that did not exist a year earlier.
insights.speaker: Walter Russell Mead (guest)
insights.so_what: A specific, verifiable real-world data point supporting the thesis of accelerating late-stage oncology drug approval/efficacy -- useful anecdotal evidence when evaluating biotech/pharma R&D pipeline momentum claims.
insights.quote: a drug that didn't exist a year ago is keeping him not just breathing but interacting with people and doing things.
